title: From typing to talking: is voice AI finally ready for the enterprise?
description:
This is a guest blogpost by John Bates, the global CEO of European-headquartered Doxis, in which he argues that the CIO needs to take natural speech interfaces more seriously.

I think the first time I told a computer what to do without touching a keyboard was when I experimented with Dragon Dictate back in the early 1990s.

We’ve come a long way since then. From the human–computer speech recognition product, we’ve progressed to voice-enabled sat navs that find hotels, Alexa providing weather updates, and Siri answering questions about football fixtures, and more. But apart from a couple of niche but successful use cases like medical transcription, we’ve never fully embraced voice as a human-computer interface method in work. Despite the compelling visions of HAL in 2001 and Samantha in Her, the idea of liberating knowledge workers from keyboards has remained largely unrealised.

It wasn’t a technology problem. Speech recognition became remarkably accurate years ago. The real obstacles were social and organisational. Talking to a computer in an open-plan office has felt a little awkward, while discussing confidential information aloud raises obvious privacy concerns. In most business environments, typing remains faster, quieter, more discreet—and, for many people, more comfortable.

But here’s an interesting thing. Generative AI may be changing the equation, as are different attitudes to using voice as an interface from younger professionals. The arrival of conversational AI via the large language model (LLM) prompt has changed what we expect from software. Rather than issuing rigid commands, people are engaging in natural dialogue with intelligent systems capable of understanding context, reasoning across information, and generate meaningful responses.

And if it already feels as though our computers are talking back to us, it is hardly a leap to start talking to them. One notable shift is the growing use of voice-enabled large language models by developers and younger knowledge workers. Rather than typing every prompt, many now speak quietly into a headset or close-range gooseneck microphone to ‘brain dump’ thoughts, draft content, or work through problems without disturbing others in the office.

Whispers in the gallery

This ‘whispering’ is increasingly being seen as a major time-saver, allowing people to task agent assistants while still in a Teams call or Zoom meeting. Voice-driven interactions now include generating code, writing tests, summarising documents, and retrieving information—all without interrupting the flow of work.

Many of us still default to the keyboard, but younger employees are developing very different habits. For Generation Z, and increasingly Generation Alpha, speaking with AI feels entirely natural, and in some organisations they already spend much of the day conversing with GPT-based assistants rather than typing prompts. As they become a larger share of the workforce, CIOs may find voice shifts from novelty to expectation.

But this is less about replacing keyboards and more about expanding the range of interfaces through which work gets done. In contexts where typing is inconvenient or impractical, voice becomes another layer of interaction, complementing, rather than displacing, existing ways of working.

Talking to not just ChatGPT, but the General Ledger

And if conversational AI continues to mature, the implications extend far beyond chatbots. The real shift is toward a world in which we interrogate and negotiate with business systems in spoken natural language, rather than SQL.

Imagine asking an ERP system why quarterly procurement costs have increased, rather than navigating dozens of reports. Or querying an invoice about its approval status, asking a contract to identify clauses that conflict with a new agreement, or asking a customer file to explain the evidence behind an insurance claim, say.

Today, business users still rely on reporting and analytics tools, adding complexity and slowing decisions. But if core business documents evolve beyond passive records, they can become ‘document intelligence’, understanding their own content, relationships, and business context. Once documents can self-classify, trigger workflows, cross-reference information, and respond to natural language queries, by text or voice, the productivity gains could be enormous.

Employees may increasingly ask documents directly for information rather than search for it. However, many workflows will still require discretion, precision, and formal verification. Financial approvals, payroll changes, procurement authorisations, and other high-risk transactions will continue to demand strong authentication and clear audit trails. And for deep work, typing will likely remain the more efficient option.

Workers will expect systems to understand their questions

But if we are moving toward a world that uses both voice and keyboards, the real shift CIOs must prepare for is that employees will expect systems to understand questions, retrieve knowledge, synthesise information, and help solve problems.

In other words, conversational AI, natural synthetic voices, intelligent documents, and a new generation comfortable speaking to machines suggest enterprise voice may finally be reaching its inflection point.

Market forecasters agree, with the Voice AI market expected to reach $22.5 billion in 2026, with so many users now interacting with LLMs by voice. Time to start taking voice a bit more seriously, I think.

The author is global CEO of European-headquartered Doxis, a document intelligence company
